title: Automaton / Uncanny Near-Human Double

source_refs.author: Ernst Jentsch
source_refs.title: On the Psychology of the Uncanny
source_refs.cultural_context: Early psychology of doubt about whether a lifelike figure is animate

source_refs.author: Sigmund Freud
source_refs.title: The Uncanny
source_refs.cultural_context: Psychoanalytic discussion of the double and of figures that are almost persons

observed_structure: A body is presented with enough human layout to be read as a person.
One or more parts are wrong, mechanical, or mismatched, so the reading fails.
The figure does not settle the doubt by ordinary speech or ordinary action.
dramatic_operations: present a body that is almost a person and not quite one
let mismatched parts block easy recognition as human
keep the double inert so likeness is felt before any deed
cinematic_affordances: a still medium or wide view long enough to compare the body with a person
one damaged or asymmetric feature held in readable light
speech replaced by a mechanical aperture, grille, or tone
no reassuring task that would classify the figure as a tool
cultural_scope: general uncanny-double figure; do not treat one psychology essay as a production recipe
misuse_risks: a robot costume played for novelty with no doubt about its status
explaining the manufacture so the uncertainty never starts
copying a famous android face, voice, or reveal

variables: whether the figure can speak words
who is forced to share the space with it

transferable_structure: a near-human body with mismatched parts stands as an uncanny double whose likeness is legible and whose intent is not yet acted
non_transferable_surface: a specific film's android design, facial appliance, or catchphrase for an artificial person
